title: Singeetham Srinivasa Rao Is 94. His New Film Has No Dialogue. Every Word Is a Song.
excerpt: Sing Geetham, the legendary director's first film in a decade, releases on June 11. Nag Ashwin produced it. DSP scored it. The script was originally pitched to Kamal Haasan before Pushpaka Vimanam.
body:
Before Pushpaka Vimanam. Before Apoorva Sagodharargal. Before Michael Madana Kama Rajan. Before any of the films that made Singeetham Srinivasa Rao one of Indian cinema's most inventive directors, there was this script — a story about a village where people speak only through song. He pitched it to Kamal Haasan. Scheduling conflicts killed it. The script sat in a drawer for decades.

Now it exists as a film. The director is 94 years old.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=jJMv6in6Ga4</youtube>


Sing Geetham, a musical fantasy produced by Nag Ashwin under Vyjayanthi Movies and Swapna Cinema, releases worldwide on June 11. It has no conventional dialogue. Every spoken word is delivered as music. Devi Sri Prasad, who composed the score, has called it the most challenging and singular experience of his career.

## A Film Where Dialogue Does Not Exist

The conceit is total. Set in Kuberapuram, a fictional town built around gold mines, the film follows a young man's journey into this isolated community. The townspeople communicate entirely through song — not in the Bollywood convention of breaking into musical numbers between dramatic scenes, but as the only medium of expression. There are no spoken lines. Every conversation, every argument, every whispered aside is composed, arranged, and performed as music.

DSP has said that even a single-word change in a line could alter the entire musical structure of a scene, making the process extraordinarily complex. The music had to be completed before shooting began — actors performed to pre-recorded compositions, which gave the film a cohesion rarely seen in Indian cinema. The result, according to Nag Ashwin, is something that feels surprisingly natural after the first few minutes.

Dubbing, however, is a different story. While the Tamil version has been completed, converting every line into other languages means painstakingly recomposing each phrase to fit a new musical metre. A pan-India release in this format is a logistical puzzle that would have defeated most production houses.

## Singeetham's Rules

Singeetham cast no stars. Not because he could not attract them — Nag Ashwin, fresh off the blockbuster Kalki 2898 AD, could have brought any name in the industry. The director's reasoning was practical: a star's persona would overwhelm the fictional world he was building. He wanted audiences to enter Kuberapuram without the baggage of existing screen identities.

The cast features newcomers Ayaan, Ahalya Bamroo, and Shalini Kondepudi. Nag Ashwin, who treated his own role as closer to an assistant director than a traditional producer, said the pre-production phase consumed nine months of writing and rigorous rehearsals. Even after that preparation, the director remained ruthlessly spontaneous on set — scrapping and rewriting his own scenes daily. When Ashwin pointed out that he was cutting material he had already written, Singeetham snapped back: "Can't I make a mistake?"

## Why This Matters for Indian Cinema

Singeetham Srinivasa Rao belongs to a lineage of Indian directors who treated cinema as a laboratory. His filmography is a catalogue of experiments: Pushpaka Vimanam had no dialogue at all. Aditya 369 was a time-travel fantasy made in 1991, decades before Indian cinema warmed to science fiction. His collaborations with Kamal Haasan pushed the actor into physical and dramatic extremes that shaped entire careers.

A fully sung feature film is not unprecedented globally — Les Misérables and Sweeney Todd come to mind — but in Indian cinema, where the line between drama and music has always been porous, no one has attempted what Sing Geetham does. The form is not a gimmick laid over a conventional story. The narrative itself is built from the music up.

## The Diaspora Angle

For Indians abroad who grew up on Singeetham's films — many of which circulated on VHS tapes in the homes of Telugu, Tamil, and Kannada diaspora families — this release carries a weight beyond commercial interest. The director's work was often underseen in its time and overdue for rediscovery. A new film, at 94, produced by the director of Kalki and scored by DSP, offers a rare chance to see a living legend operate at the frontier of what Indian film can do.

Sing Geetham arrives in cinemas next Wednesday, June 11. Whether mainstream audiences will accept a film with no spoken dialogue is an open question. But the fact that it exists at all is the point.

*Sources: Tupaki, Gulte, TeluguOne, NRI Page, Wikipedia*
